> There are lot of uuid handling code in Bluetooth, should BT use this library?

I'm unfamiliar regarding the Bluetooth use of the UUID. I see it uses 16 and 32 bits partial UUIDs, which are not defined in [RFC 9562](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9562).
We could add a couple of defines similar to the ones in the bluetooth driver ([`BT_UUID_INIT_128`](https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/doxygen/html/group__bt__uuid.html#ga1a840adf4bc06cf2cd5dbeb0c868374b) for example) to ease the transition.

AFAIK at least the 16- and 32-bit Bluetooth UUIDs don't follow any non-Bluetooth standard. The way the Bluetooth core specification deals with these, is that in practice everything is a 128-bit UUID, however UUIDs which are derived from the so-called Bluetooth Base UUID can be compressed into 16- and 32-bit formats (and these again expanded back into 128 bit format). I have a feeling we'll need to keep the Bluetooth UUID API separate, but some proper research into their compatibility with these RFC specs needs to be done. We might at most e.g. provide conversion functions to convert back and forth between bt_uuid_t and uuid_t.

The issue with the endianness is that the UUID spec defines UUID only as big-endian.
The interpretation of little-endian UUID is not universal.
From my understanding here are our options for the UUID:
- Standard big-endian representation: `00112233-4455-6677-8899-AABBCCDDEEFF`
- little-endian representation inverting each block: `33221100-5544-7766-9988-FFEEDDCCBBAA`
- little-endian representation inverting the full UUID: `FFEEDDCC-BBAA-9988-7766-554433221100`
- little-endian representation for Microsoft COM GUIs representation: `33221100-5544-7766-8899-AABBCCDDEEFF`

I'm not sure which of those little-endian notations is used in the Bluetooth module. 
However, from my very superficial research, I think the last one is the more widely adopted. It's also the only one referenced in the standard.
Yes, if we follow the COM GUID representation the last two should not be swapped.

As far as I can tell, there's only a single possible represenation: 
```
The formal definition of the UUID string representation is provided by the following ABNF [[RFC5234](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5234)]:

UUID     = 4hexOctet "-"
           2hexOctet "-"
           2hexOctet "-"
           2hexOctet "-"
           6hexOctet
hexOctet = HEXDIG HEXDIG
DIGIT    = %x30-39
HEXDIG   = DIGIT / "A" / "B" / "C" / "D" / "E" / "F"

Note that the alphabetic characters may be all uppercase, all lowercase, or mixed case, as per [Section 2.3](https://rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5234#section-2.3) of [[RFC5234](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5234)]. An example UUID using this textual representation from the above ABNF is shown in [Figure 1](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9562#sampleStringUUID).

f81d4fae-7dec-11d0-a765-00a0c91e6bf6
```

So regardless of version, it will always be `xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx` and since UUIDs are always Big endian (in RFC9562) then that represenation works with all versions.

Summary of what changed
- Replaced the MFIFO-based prepare pipeline with an explicitly ordered singly linked list in subsys/bluetooth/controller/ll_sw/ull.c.
  - New pipeline structure: pool-backed nodes storing a next pointer plus struct lll_event.
  - Enqueue is now order-aware by ticks_at_expire and treats resume events specially.
  - Dequeue/iteration now uses void** as an iterator cursor (NULL means start/end), replacing uint8_t indices.
- API updates:
  - ull_prepare_dequeue_iter signature changed from uint8_t* to void** (see subsys/bluetooth/controller/ll_sw/lll.h). All call sites in Nordic and OpenISA LLL updated accordingly.
- Nordic LLL changes (subsys/bluetooth/controller/ll_sw/nordic/lll/lll.c):
  - prepare_dequeue_iter_ready_get now filters out aborted, resume, and defer entries.
  - lll_disable, lll_prepare_resolve, and preempt reworked for the new iterator. Notably, the prior workaround that aborted earlier prepares to make room for “short” prepares has been removed; ordering is handled by the list.
- OpenISA LLL changes (subsys/bluetooth/controller/ll_sw/openisa/lll/lll.c):
  - Equivalent iterator and control-flow updates to match the new pipeline semantics.
- Scan updates:
  - lll_scan.h adds a persistent lll_prepare_param field when advanced scheduler is enabled.
  - lll_scan.c and lll_scan_aux.c copy timing fields into lll->prepare_param and pass that to mayfly, avoiding lifetime issues from passing a stack/local param.
- Initialization:
  - The pipeline memory is initialized in init_reset via mem_init; MFIFO prep init removed.

Why this is a good change
- Correctness and determinism: The prepare pipeline is now ordered by scheduling time instead of FIFO plus ad-hoc aborts. This removes the previous “abort to reorder” workaround and should reduce spurious aborts and reschedules, especially for short preemptors.
- Simpler preemption logic: Preempt handling is cleaner; instead of scanning/aborting earlier entries to accommodate a short event, the ordered structure ensures correct sequencing.
- Safer parameter passing in scan paths: Copying timing/param state into lll->prepare_param before scheduling mayfly avoids dangling references to transient stack data.
- Clearer iteration semantics: Using a pointer cursor for ull_prepare_dequeue_iter is a better fit for list traversal than synthetic indices, reducing off-by-one/overflow risks.

Things to double-check
- Concurrency/atomicity: MFIFO provided a well-tested queue; the new list relies on mem_acquire/mem_release and pointer manipulation. Ensure all accesses occur under the same context/locking assumptions as before and that no ISR/LLL context can mutate the list concurrently with ULL.
- Ordering conditions: The insertion logic relies on ticker_ticks_diff_get and MSBIT checks. These are notoriously subtle with wrap-around; unit/soak tests around boundary conditions (near wrap and equal times) would be valuable.
- Resume event handling: The enqueue code treats resume specially (often appended). The dequeue path enqueues at most two non-resume events before switching behavior; verify this preserves prior fairness/progress guarantees and doesn’t starve resumes or normal events under load.
- Memory footprint: Each pipeline node adds a pointer over the previous structure. The increase is small but present; confirm this fits tight controller builds.
- API ripple: All call sites appear updated for the new iterator type in Nordic and OpenISA; ensure there are no out-of-tree or less commonly built targets relying on the old signature.

Overall assessment
- This is a solid improvement. It addresses a known limitation of the FIFO pipeline, removes complex workarounds, and makes scheduling behavior more predictable. With careful validation around concurrency and time-diff edge cases, it looks like a positive and maintainable change.

@soburi thanks for your update. I agree we should discuss this design-level issue first.

The "compound" concept appears in both edtlib and dtlib:

- in edtlib, we have the "compound" type in the bindings syntax, which I believe historically was added mainly to document and capture complex cases that we couldn't express in our existing syntax
- in dtlib, the "compound" type in the DTS syntax parser exists as a catch-all for properties that we don't have special-case support for. It's important to remember that from the perspective of the DT specification, all properties are just byte arrays, and the source encoding was ignored by the consumer of the DTB as defined in chapter 5 of the specification. Zephyr is unique among operating systems in that it reads the DTS directly, of course. The dtlib parser has several special case "types" encoded in the dtlib.Type enum. For properties that don't fit in any special case, we can still access the byte array value, and the property is exposed as type dtlib.Type.COMPOUND.

I will try to be clear about which case I am talking about when we think about nexus nodes:

- in edtlib, our existing bindings syntax doesn't have a concept of a nexus node and so the only way we can name such properties as `<specifier>-map` in the bindings is with type 'compound' in the bindings syntax
- in dtlib, we are specifically concerned with the properties defined in section 2.5 of the specification, whose format and syntax fits into these dtlib types:

  - `<specifier>-map`: the specification describes properties of dtlib.Type.PHANDLES_AND_NUMS, not dtlib.Type.COMPOUND
  - `<specifier>-map-mask`: dtlib.Type.NUMS
  - `<specifier>-map-pass-thru`: dtlib.Type.NUMS
  - `#<specifier>-cells`: dtlib.Type.NUM

I think that since our dtlib parser already seems to have the right dtlib.Type special cases to handle nexus nodes, we probably don't need any dtlib changes to handle these. However, since the edtlib library doesn't have support for this pattern in its bindings syntax, I think we have two choices:

1. extend the bindings syntax to add new special case types for `<specifier>-map`
2. add special-case handling for this chapter of the devicetree specification, similarly to how we handled GPIO hogs

I think choice 2 is best, because this is a special case that is defined directly in the specification. We already allow edtlib to handle these types of special cases for things like the interrupt tree (DT specification section 2.4), major properties like `reg` and `compatible` (specification section 2.3), etc.

I outlined a way that I think we can implement option 2 that checks that the user's devicetree matches the requirements of specification section 2.5, Nexus Nodes and Specifier Mapping, in my previous review comment.

The polarity detection logic at lines 564-569 reads the current polarity from hardware to determine which edge triggered the interrupt, but when COUNTER_CAPTURE_BOTH_EDGES is configured, LL_TIM_IC_GetPolarity returns LL_TIM_IC_POLARITY_BOTHEDGE. This means the callback will be invoked with COUNTER_CAPTURE_BOTH_EDGES flag, making it impossible for the callback to distinguish whether it was triggered by a rising or falling edge. For both-edge capture, the STM32 hardware doesn't provide information about which edge caused the trigger. This limitation should be documented, or an alternative approach should be used (such as reading the current pin state to infer the edge direction).

w.r.t. the thread issue, that's also something we are trying to deal with in the LE Audio implementation, where we have many cases of attribute values that may be changed locally or remotely. In those cases we are generally dealing with

1. Local application is reading or writing to modify a local value. This may occur in any thread, and any remote device may be writing or reading to the same value in the BT RX thread. For trivial values it's not a big issue, but for larger values that may need to be formatted on air, we use a mutex to lock the attribute, where remote access is guarded with a small timeout (e.g. 10ms in the read or write callbacks), and local access are guarded with K_NO_WAIT and will return an error immediately if the local change cannot occurs due to the mutex being locked
2. Notifications sent based on value changes are usually done in the system workqueue. The reason for this is that whenever a change is happening, we may not have free ATT buffers to send/enqueue the notification immediately. Handling the notifications in the system workqueue with a dirty-bit approach allows us to easily implement a retry-if-no-buffers solution. Any access to the resources here is also guarded, and if the mutex cannot be taken immediately we simply retry with a delay. 

We are not yet completely at a place where everything is properly guarded, or if the current solution is optimal, but it does work a lot better than doing nothing :)

`K_SECONDS(timeout)` is passed a `double`. `K_SECONDS()` expands to integer tick conversion macros and should be given an integer duration; passing floating-point can truncate and may trigger warnings or incorrect timeouts. Consider converting explicitly to milliseconds and using `K_MSEC()`.

The file appears to start with a UTF-8 BOM character before the shebang (``/invisible), which can break the kernel shebang parsing and also violates Zephyr’s non-ASCII guidance. Remove the BOM so the very first bytes are `#!`.

Kconfig symbol has no type, so it defaults to `bool`, but it’s given a numeric default/range. This will be rejected by Kconfig parsing. Declare it as an `int` (optionally without a prompt if it’s meant to be hidden).

CMake style: command names should be lowercase in Zephyr, and using `file(GLOB ...)` makes the build sensitive to stale CMake state. Since the sources are known, list them explicitly in `target_sources()` with 2-space indentation.

`wait_for_async_jobs()` claims to return the *first* failed process’ exit code, but the loop overwrites `exit_code` on every failure. This can hide the initial failure reason and makes debugging flaky.

The load guard variable is named `COMPILE_UTILS_LOADED`, but this file is `common_utils.sh`. This increases the chance of accidental collisions with other sourced helpers and makes the intent unclear.

Installing/uninstalling Python packages at test runtime is fragile (requires network access, writable environment, and can break hermetic CI). It’s safer for the harness to *check* the Bumble version and fail with a clear message if the dependency isn’t satisfied.
`inquiry_mode` is an integer/enum-like value; using `is` performs identity comparison, which is not reliable for numeric values. Use `==` for the mode checks to avoid intermittent behavior.

`br_discover_sem` can be given both when the target device is found *and* again on the discovery timeout callback. When the device is found early, that extra give can leave the semaphore in a signaled state and make subsequent `peer_device_discovery()` calls return immediately (this test calls discovery multiple times in `test_02_limited_discovery`). Reset the semaphore before starting a new discovery.

`timeout_ms` is a `uint64_t`, but `%llu` assumes `unsigned long long`. On LP64 platforms `uint64_t` is often `unsigned long`, which can trigger format warnings/errors. Cast explicitly (or use PRIu64).

If `--peer_bd_address` is malformed, the test keeps running with an uninitialized/zero address, which tends to fail later with a much less actionable assertion. Since this is a mandatory option, fail fast from the cmdline callback (native_sim provides `nsi_exit()`).

The driver disables RX interrupts after receiving a single frame and only flushes the UART FIFO once during init. If a board configuration sets this value too small (e.g. 1), incoming UART frames can trigger out-of-bounds writes in the driver, corrupting adjacent kernel memory and allowing a malicious or compromised sensor module to crash the system or potentially gain code execution. `efi_get_gop_mode()` treats the GOP mode as valid as long as width/height are non-zero, but it can still return a zero pitch. A zero (or otherwise invalid) pitch will cause the GOP display driver to compute incorrect offsets and potentially scribble memory. Consider validating `efi->gop_pitch` (e.g., non-zero, and optionally >= width) before returning true.

`efi_gop_write()` does not validate `desc->width <= desc->pitch` or that the write region stays within the framebuffer bounds (x/y + width/height). Many display drivers in-tree add `__ASSERT()`s and return `-EINVAL` on invalid descriptors/coordinates (see `drivers/display/display_dummy.c`). Without these checks this driver can write past the framebuffer and corrupt memory.

`efi_gop_read()` similarly lacks validation of `desc` (width vs pitch) and bounds checks for x/y + region size. This can read past the framebuffer and potentially leak/corrupt memory via the destination buffer. Add the same assertions and `-EINVAL` guards used by other drivers (e.g., `display_dummy.c`).

The bootloader accepts both `PixelRedGreenBlueReserved8BitPerColor` and `PixelBlueGreenRedReserved8BitPerColor`, but the runtime driver exposes only `PIXEL_FORMAT_ARGB_8888` (which corresponds to a specific byte order). If the GOP is in the RGB-reserved order, colors will be swapped at runtime because the pixel format isn’t recorded/preserved. Either restrict to the byte order that matches `PIXEL_FORMAT_ARGB_8888`, or store the GOP PixelFormat in `efi_arg` and have the driver select/convert accordingly.

`struct efi_boot_arg` stores GOP resolution/pitch and framebuffer base/size, but it does not record the GOP PixelFormat/byte order. Since the display driver advertises `PIXEL_FORMAT_ARGB_8888`, the pixel byte order matters for correct colors. Consider adding a field to carry the GOP pixel format (or a boolean for BGR vs RGB) so the runtime driver can validate/handle the framebuffer layout correctly.

The framebuffer is mapped with `k_mem_map_phys_bare(..., K_MEM_PERM_RW)` but no cache mode is specified. Many drivers mapping MMIO / framebuffers explicitly request `K_MEM_CACHE_NONE` to avoid cache incoherency (e.g., `drivers/ethernet/eth_dwmac_mmu.c`). Consider adding an explicit cache mode flag appropriate for a framebuffer mapping (often `K_MEM_CACHE_NONE`, or an arch-specific write-combining mode if available).

Before using `width/height/pitch` to write into the framebuffer (including the gray fill loop), the driver should validate that the mapped `fb_size` is large enough for the claimed mode (e.g., `pitch * height * 4` bytes, with `pitch >= width`). As written, a corrupted/incorrect GOP mode could lead to out-of-bounds writes into whatever follows the mapped region.

Tested this on the Cortex-M7 of an **NXP FRDM-IMX95** (`imx95_evk/mimx9596/m7`, Zephyr 4.4.0) under Linux remoteproc (NXP BSP kernel 6.18.2, `imx_rproc` + `virtio_rpmsg_bus`). It works well once three small things are addressed. I carried the PR as an out-of-tree module to try it, with each fix as a separate commit written against Zephyr-tree paths: https://github.com/beriberikix/zephyr-rproc-ipc

**Results on hardware**

- Echo on an `rpmsg-raw` endpoint (`/dev/rpmsgN` on Linux): 205/205 messages of 1–496 bytes byte-exact, ~1.3 MiB/s round-trip, including across three remoteproc stop/start cycles.
- Two endpoints on one vdev: Linux creates a channel for each (0x400, 0x401), and each `/dev/rpmsgN` reaches the right one (100/100 each).
- On top of it I also tried an IPC service backend and an MCUmgr SMP transport (below). A real application (a [Pouch](https://github.com/golioth/pouch) session to Golioth) runs over it end to end.

**Fixes that were needed on i.MX95**

1. **Resource table location** ([91b8df6](https://github.com/beriberikix/zephyr-rproc-ipc/commit/91b8df678dabbb4205b0c5d15dea9597a642228c)). Linux's i.MX remoteproc copies the table into its fixed `rsc-table` reserved region and then reads/writes that copy, so `rproc_virtio_wait_remote_ready()` never sees `DRIVER_OK` if the remote uses its linked table. I added an optional `memory-region` to `openamp,resource-table`: when set, the table is copied there (and cache-flushed) before first use, and all lookups point into the copy. This is what `CONFIG_OPENAMP_COPY_RSC_TABLE` does for the existing sample.
2. **Doorbell** ([0d7dd8e](https://github.com/beriberikix/zephyr-rproc-ipc/commit/0d7dd8e700d57052e19e28579a86c90104852e2b)). `rvdev_notify()` sends `mbox_send_dt(tx, NULL)`. On the i.MX MU a NULL message is a general-purpose interrupt, while Linux takes vring kicks as data messages, so the name-service announcement is never seen: no channel is created. Sending the notify id as data when `mbox_mtu_get_dt() > 0` fixes it (confirmed by reverting just this change).
3. **`.resource_table` placement** ([56d469f](https://github.com/beriberikix/zephyr-rproc-ipc/commit/56d469f7b17a140dd74dd8b1e788bd579d019cc5)). Nothing places the section, so it lands as an orphan with a linker warning. The existing SoC snippets (e.g. `soc/nxp/imx/rsc_table.ld`) are gated on the legacy `CONFIG_OPENAMP_RSC_TABLE`. I placed it from the driver's CMake with `SUBALIGN(8)` and made `OPENAMP_RESOURCE_TABLE` depend on `!OPENAMP_RSC_TABLE`, since both define `resource_table`.

**Other notes from bring-up** (not blocking for me)

- The vrings need fixed `device-address` values: `rvdev_init()` reads `vring[i].da` before waiting for the host, so the default of -1 cannot work. (From reading the code, not tested.)
- Carveout names must equal the Linux reserved-memory node names (`vdev0vring0`, `vdev0vring1`, `vdevbuffer` here). From my reading of `rproc_handle_carveout()`, a name Linux does not know makes it allocate a fresh carveout rather than use the reserved region. (Also from reading the code.) This might be worth a line in the binding docs.
- `rvdev_init()` blocks `POST_KERNEL` init until the host sets `DRIVER_OK`. Harmless when Linux loads the core (~60 ms here), but it might be worth doing in the rx thread.
- `zephyr,priority` is declared in `openamp,rpmsg-virtio-device.yaml`, but the driver only uses `CONFIG_RPMSG_VDEV_THREAD_PRIORITY`. The priority matters: endpoint callbacks run on that thread, and in my application it has to sit below the app's work queue.
- `z_rproc_get_vdev(config->idx)` matches the instance index against the vdev node's `reg`, so `reg` has to equal the DT instance number.
- `metal_io_init(&data->mr_rsc_table, rsc_table, (metal_phys_addr_t *)rsc_table, ...)` passes the table itself as the physmap, which looks unintended.
- The second "failed to init vring 0" error message is for vring 1.

**Built on top** (same repo, in case it is useful for where this goes next)

- An IPC service backend, `zephyr,ipc-rproc-rpmsg`, that wraps the `rpmsg_device` from this driver. Endpoints are announced via the name service. Since the NS has no ack, `bound` fires on the first message from the host.
- `MCUMGR_TRANSPORT_IPC`, raw SMP over an IPC endpoint with reassembly. `smpmgr` works through a small Linux UDP relay, with packets of ~1.9 KB in both directions.

A runtime DAA triggered by hot join will therefore silently disable IBIs previously enabled on existing targets while the driver still treats those IBIs as enabled. Limit DISEC to newly assigned targets (for example with directed CCCs), or do it only in the bus-initialization phase that already broadcasts DISEC before DAA.

The sent variable answers “have we already attempted this server for this query?” while pending answers “is there still an in-flight request to this server right now?”

So for one server, the state typically moves like this:

1. Initial: sent=0, pending=0, failed=0
2. Query transmitted: sent=1, pending=1
3. Reply or timeout/failure handled: sent=1, pending=0, and maybe failed=1

That difference is important because after a server stops being active, we still need to remember that it was already tried. If we only had pending, then once a timeout or negative reply cleared it, that server would look “unused” and fallback could send to it again.

`bt_hogp_device_register()` uses the `callbacks` pointer as the “registered” flag (`if (callbacks) ...`), but then assigns `callbacks = param->cb` without requiring it to be non-NULL. If `param->cb` is NULL, the service can be registered successfully while later APIs (e.g. `bt_hogp_device_send_report()`) will return -ESRCH and connection callbacks won’t run (`hogp_dev_connected` bails out on `!callbacks`). Use a separate registration state variable (or require `param->cb != NULL`) so registration and callback presence are not conflated.

`bt_hogp_device_unregister()` may double-unref `bt_conn` objects: it calls `bt_conn_disconnect()` (async) for each stored connection, then immediately iterates `connections[]` and `bt_conn_unref()`s any non-NULL entries. If the disconnect callback (`hogp_dev_disconnected`) runs after the manual unref loop, it will unref the same connection again. To avoid a potential refcount underflow/use-after-free, either unref+NULL the slots synchronously in `unregister()` (and make the disconnect cb ignore missing slots), or defer unref until the disconnect callback completes.

that a good question .here are  two possible approaches:

  Option A: Pure HIDS Service (bt_hids_*)
  - Register GATT attribute table, forward all events to app
  - App owns all state (protocol mode, suspend, report caching)
  - App must handle GATT read/write semantics directly
  - Simpler implementation, but more burden on app developers

  - Profile manages internal state, app receives high-level notifications
  - App focuses on HID business logic, not GATT details
  - Follows the pattern of VCP (manages volume state), nRF bt_hids
    (manages protocol mode per-connection), and BTstack hids_device
    (stores protocol_mode + suspend internally, emits events)

 What the profile layer currently provides beyond a raw service:

  | Aspect | Pure Service | This Profile |
  |--------|-------------|-------------|
  | Protocol Mode | App stores + returns on read | Profile stores, serves reads, notifies app of changes |
  | Suspend | App stores + decides behavior | Profile tracks state, app queries via is_suspended() |
  | GET_REPORT | App manages GATT read buffer | Profile handles GATT, calls app synchronously (CTS pattern) |
  | Security | App configures permissions | Profile enforces via depends on BT_SMP + encrypted attrs |
  | Connections | App tracks refs | Profile manages lifecycle, prevents double-unref races |
  | Host discovery | App does manual GATT discovery | bt_hogp_host_connect() orchestrates HIDS+DIS+BAS (#109579) |

  I believe Option B (profile) is more useful for application developers — it's the approach taken by nRF Connect SDK, BTstack, and ESP-IDF for their HID Device implementations. None of them expose raw GATT

A later standalone Read Blob Request for the same report reuses `rd_buf` indefinitely because `rd_ctx == ctx`, so `get_report` is not called and stale report data is returned. This also contradicts the public guarantee that the callback runs once per read. Track the expected continuation offset (and clear the cache when the read completes), and refresh whenever the incoming offset is not the next blob of the active read.

This write path does not require a tracked HID connection. If `BT_HIDS_MAX_CONNECTIONS` is lower than `BT_MAX_CONN` and all slots are occupied, an additional Host can still write Output/Feature Reports and invoke the application callback, despite the Kconfig contract that excess connections are denied Report access. Reject writes when `conn_lookup(conn)` returns NULL, as the read and stateful characteristic paths do.

This managed CCC write callback accepts and stores every 16-bit value. Since the associated characteristic supports notifications only, values such as `BT_GATT_CCC_INDICATE` or reserved bits are invalid; accepting them leaves a nonsensical subscription state and reports `enabled == false` as if the write succeeded. Restrict writes to disabled or notify.

The lookup and allocation are separate operations, so this can race with `hids_connected()`: both callers can observe no entry and then claim different slots for the same connection. One Host can therefore consume two slots and cause another valid Host to be denied service. Serialize lookup-and-claim or make allocation atomically detect an existing connection.

`hids.registered` remains true while connection slots are being freed. If a connection callback runs after an earlier slot was cleared but before this assignment, `hids_connected()` can allocate that slot and the cleanup loop will not revisit it, retaining a connection reference after unregistration. Make registration state synchronized across callback/application contexts and clear it immediately after successful GATT unregistration, before releasing slots.

`CONFIG_BT_HIDS_MAX_REPORT_LEN` is documented as the upper bound in both directions, but this API only rejects NULL and zero-length payloads. With a sufficiently large negotiated MTU, a caller can send a report larger than the configured maximum. Reject `len > CONFIG_BT_HIDS_MAX_REPORT_LEN` as invalid.

The per-connection API contract says an unsubscribed Host produces `-EINVAL`, but `bt_gatt_notify_cb()` only performs that check when the independently configurable `CONFIG_BT_GATT_ENFORCE_SUBSCRIPTION` is enabled. With that option disabled, this sends an Input Report to the specified connection even when its CCC is disabled. Enforce the HIDS contract explicitly before notifying.

`hex2bin()` writes into the destination incrementally before returning 0 on an invalid digit. For example, `hids value 3 0G` reports an error but can still overwrite the first byte while leaving the old length, changing subsequent GET_REPORT results. Parse into a temporary buffer and copy it only after successful validation.

The current change exposes only the HIDS service and explicitly leaves HIDS+BAS+DIS composition to the application, while the PR title/description still claim a `bt_hogp_device_*` profile layer under `subsys/bluetooth/profiles/hogp/` and four commits. Either add that advertised profile layer or update the PR scope, title, table, and commit list to describe this HIDS-only three-commit change.

The CAS publishes `conn` before `protocol_mode` and `suspended` are initialized, so `conn_lookup()` can expose stale state to a concurrent GATT callback. Registration can also race the connected callback: both paths can observe the connection as untracked and claim separate slots, while the plain state fields are concurrently accessed by GATT writes and public getters. Protect lookup, allocation, initialization, release, and state access with one synchronization strategy, and publish each connection only after its state is initialized so it owns exactly one slot.

A nonzero write offset is an ATT Invalid Offset, but this combined check returns Invalid Attribute Length for both an offset error and a size error. We could remove the automatic fallback, but then each driver that uses fast GPIO would need to add an override attribute to DT and IMO that would be much more confusing to document and consistently implement in every downstream driver.

We could add `CONFIG_GPIO_FAST_BACKEND_atmel_sam0` to Kconfig, but this would break with existing naming scheme (i.e. no manufacturer name and all caps: `CONFIG_GPIO_SAM0`). The existing DT names unfortunately does not mirror the Kconfig options.

We could instead implement the fallback by requiring every single GPIO driver to implement every function regardless, like this, but this is very messy (would requiring updating every driver)

OK, there's 3 parts here:

#### Frequency

Frequency is determined from the provided `GPIO_FAST_CPU_FREQ` var (which comes from DT). A driver uses `GPIO_FAST_NS_TO_CYCLES()` to convert from nanoseconds to cycles (this macro uses the correct frequency from `GPIO_FAST_CPU_FREQ`) at compile time.

Currently, this only supports one frequency, so backends need to implement `gpio_fast_pre_stream_<compat>()`/`gpio_fast_post_stream_<compat>()` if clock control is enabled to ensure the frequency is correct. We could add a `CONFIG_GPIO_FAST_CPU_FREQ` to Kconfig to allow the user to override the frequency determined at compile time. We could make it possible for a driver compile for multiple frequency options at compile time (and branch at runtime before the timing-critical section), but this would be in a followup PR.

#### SOC-specific Operation Cycle Counts

The cycle counts per operation are specific to the permutation of 1) the SOC, 2) the particular GPIO peripheral, and 3) the specific implementation written in the backend for manipulating that peripheral. Frequency does not affect this count, although we subtract these counts from the result of `GPIO_FAST_NS_TO_CYCLES()` at compile time to determine the `nop` timing.

Since these are SOC-specific/only on-SOC GPIO peripherals, I think it makes most sense to add an `#ifdef` per SOC that adjust these cycle counts by SOC (same way different SOCs are handled in the general GPIO drivers). I don't think it makes sense to put these in DT, as they are specific to the function implementations written in the driver, not generalization to a SOC as a whole. I have already done this one one case: the STM32 backend has relies on `CONFIG_SOC_SERIES_STM32F1X` and adjusts timings/implementation based on that (which is the same way it works in the general STM32 GPIO driver).

I will work on adding these SOC `#ifdef`s.

#### Drive Strength and Other Peripheral-Specific Features

The drive strength does not affect the number of cycles required to set/read a GPIO register, so it does not affect the cycle timings as implemented. Most protocols, like the WS2812, have some tolerances for different slew rates; in my testing I did not need to offset for slew rate differences between GPIO peripherals for WS2812. For other applications that require more precise timing requirements, we can easily add constants like `GPIO_FAST_SET_SLEW_TIME_NS_<compat>_gpio` that drivers can make use of if necessary (can add in followup PRs). The actual computation of the timings is up to the downstream driver; it uses a combination of the provided frequency, nanosecond conversion helpers, and set/clear/toggle timings to do this. Additionally, drivers/users can override timings in DT with optional per-downstream-driver parameters like `delay-t0h` like the WS2812 driver offers (see #111218).

There is nothing restricting us from adding more DT params (like `fast-gpio-drive-strength` or `fast-gpio-stm32-drive-strength`) in followup PRs that would be consumed by `gpio_fast_configure_<compat>_gpio()`. Since these would go in DT, they can be known at compile time and affect timing constants (like `GPIO_FAST_SET_SLEW_TIME_NS_<compat>_gpio` above). Since the timings need to be known at compile time, I don't think you can switch drive strength at runtime if it affects the timings. I also can't see a reason to need to switch drive strength modes more quickly than the standard GPIO API, although that could easily be added as a method to the backend.

OK, I took a look at this. To recap, the current solution I have implemented:

1. User enables `CONFIG_GPIO_FAST_OUT_OF_TREE_BACKEND`
2. User provides `zephyr_gpio_fast_impl_oot.h`

The tracing backend seems to work _exactly_ like this (`CONFIG_TRACING_CUSTOM` + `zephyr_custom_tracing.h`):
https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/c01ba2033999385e5306b38deddc2fe9501daf74/include/zephyr/tracing/tracing.h#L19-L28

In contrast, the logging backends rely on choosing at runtime:

1. OOT module defines a logging backend struct with function pointers for its API (e.g. `log_backend_msg_process`).
2. OOT module registers it with `LOG_BACKEND_DEFINE()`, which places the struct into a dedicated linker section via `STRUCT_SECTION_ITERABLE`.
3. At runtime, the logging core iterates all backends in that linker section using `STRUCT_SECTION_FOREACH` and dispatches log messages through the function pointers.
4. No in-tree header modification or `#include` of OOT code is needed. The linker collects everything automatically.

This will not work because we need the linker and preprocessor to find all of the methods/macros at compile time (no function pointers).

1. User creates a header with the backend-specific headers and `#define` statements.
2. User includes the header through a CMake helper like `include_fast_gpio_backend(file)`. This helper can be called multiple times.
3. CMake generates a header that includes each files specified by `include_fast_gpio_backend()`.
4. Main Fast GPIO header includes this generated header.

This method would allow a user to include multiple backend headers without needing to assemble them into one header or include them from one header. No. Respectfully using a "dummy MAC" address during iface_init as a workaround introduces several silent failure modes and defeats the entire purpose of the original validation feature (commit 481035c):

1. Defeats the Validation Logic: If the driver populates a dummy MAC during init just to satisfy an early check, the Ethernet L2 layer will validate a placeholder. If the firmware subsequently fails to load or fail to retrieve the actual OTP MAC during eth->start(), the interface will stay up using an invalid or duplicated dummy MAC. This brings us right back to the original issue where invalid MACs pass without notice.
2. Race Conditions with Network Management: If the interface initialized with a dummy MAC is exposed to user-space or network management daemons (like WPA Supplicant) before eth->start() finishes swapping it with the real burned-in address, it can cause race conditions where upper layers cache or bind to the wrong hardware address.
3. Power Management Violations: To avoid a dummy MAC, the driver would have to power up the chip, clock the SPI/QSPI buses, boot the companion firmware, and read the OTP during iface_init. Forcing this during early system boot—when the interface might not even be administratively brought up until much later—violates basic low-power embedded design principles.

Delaying validation until the device is actually entering the start phase ensures we are validating the real hardware state without introducing side-channel workarounds.

> as long as the iface is not up, the mac address can be changed at any time with `net_mgmt(NET_REQUEST_ETHERNET_SET_MAC_ADDRESS`, applications or subsystems can't expect that a mac address doesn't change when it is not up.

To look at this from the perspective of upper-layer applications: many subsystems do not explicitly set a MAC address. Instead, they rely entirely on the L2/driver to fetch the authentic OTP address from the hardware. They expect that the moment net_if_up() completes, the interface's MAC is its finalized, true identity.

If a driver uses a dummy MAC placeholder during iface_init to satisfy an early L2 check, and then updates it to the real OTP address inside eth->start(), we create a critical timing hazard for things like DHCP, IPv6 DAD, or WPA Supplicant. If any upper-layer network event triggers or binds to the interface identity right as the state transitions to UP, it risks capturing or caching the transient dummy MAC instead of the real burned-in address.

Overall, using a dummy MAC to bypass a check during iface_init only to overwrite it during eth->start() is entirely pointless for those drivers/devices that actually start the operations in start.

> We could also have a Kconfig that drivers, that have a late setting of the mac, can select and only then check the mac after start and check the mac address otherwise before start. Or then leave it to the driver inside start to check it.

Checking after start() is a strict superset of checking before it: a MAC set in init is still valid after start() (start does not clobber it), so the after-start check catches every statically-misconfigured MAC the before-start check would, and additionally handles drivers that only learn their address during bring-up (nRF70 reads it from OTP once firmware boots). The before-start check catches a subset and cannot validate late-MAC drivers at all.

On avoiding a power-on with a bad MAC: the drivers where powering on is actually expensive (companion chips that clock a bus and boot firmware) are precisely the late-MAC drivers, which have no address to check before start() — so an early check cannot help them. The drivers where you can check early (MAC set in init) are on-die MACs where bring-up is cheap. The early check only ever fires where it does not matter, and is impossible where it would. On top of that, a statically-invalid MAC is a deterministic DTS/build error: you hit it once on the first bring-up during development and get a clear log; in production the address is valid and the path is never taken. There is no recurring runtime cost being traded away.

Given that, a Kconfig only adds a second code path and doubles the behavior we have to reason about and test, for a knob almost no driver would set. So I'd keep it as a single unconditional check right after start() returns.

Right - the itcm/dtcm node labels only exist in the CM55 devicetree (the CM33 uses separate itcm_m33s/dtcm_m33s nodes), so the `DT_NODE_EXISTS()` guard already scopes these two entries to the CM55 build. There is no extra `CONFIG_CPU_CORTEX_M55` guard on them; `DT_NODE_EXISTS` alone is sufficient. I kept the comment above the block to make that reasoning explicit.

No CM55 code reads the CM33 code/data regions. The CM55 runs its own image out of its TCMs and the CM55 code/shared windows, and all cross-core shared data goes through the dedicated allocatable-shared windows: `m55_allocatable_shared` (mapped on the CM55) and `m33_allocatable_shared` / SHARED_MEMORY_33 (no core guard, so it stays mapped on both cores). The M33S_CODE / M33_CODE entries are CM33 code-in-SRAM windows that the CM55 neither executes nor reads, so dropping both exec and read access on the CM55 is intentional - it recovers an HW MPU region without removing any access the CM55 actually uses.

The benefit is in binding the argument at all, not in the `const`. This macro is already a statement expression, so give `data` a name there and use it in all three places:

```c
#define k_fifo_peek_next(fifo, data)                                                               \
	({                                                                                         \
		void *fpt_data = (data);                                                           \
		SYS_PORT_TRACING_OBJ_FUNC_ENTER(k_fifo, peek_next, fifo, fpt_data);                 \
		void *fpt_ret = k_queue_peek_next(&(fifo)->_queue, fpt_data);                       \
		SYS_PORT_TRACING_OBJ_FUNC_EXIT(k_fifo, peek_next, fifo, fpt_data, fpt_ret);         \
		fpt_ret;                                                                           \
	})
```

Digging in, each one pointed at a root cause worth fixing where the problem actually is rather than accommodating it per board, so I split them out. Here is how I would land each piece:

* **remove hardcoded TIMESLICE_SIZE default** (7565efb): keep this, it is the one change here that genuinely belongs in the Bee SoC. A SoC should not pin the scheduler timeslice; the kernel's 20 ms default is fine and this just stops overriding it.

* **tune SysTick min-timeout-cycles to 30** (286ac2b): the fixed 30-cycle floor is a symptom. MIN_DELAY is a wall-clock property (it must exceed the longest the SysTick IRQ can stay masked), so a hardcoded cycle count is wrong on any clock rate, not only 32 kHz. #113083 derives it from the cycle rate in the driver (about 1 cycle at 32 kHz), which removes the need for a per-board dts override and also lets the driver program sub-tick LOAD values again, fixing the dticks=2 double-fire that timeslicing exposed on your platform. With that in, this commit and the overrides can drop, and TIMESLICING no longer needs to be disabled.

* **accommodate 32 kHz SysTick in timer_behavior** (1903a43): the test's tolerances were hand-tuned percentages with per-board exceptions, and 32 kHz needed yet another. #113053 recomputes the drift and jitter bounds from the clock (one tick, one period), so coarse clocks widen automatically and no board .conf overrides are needed. (Upstream just had to add an Infineon lptimer exception to the very same knob, which is the churn this avoids.)

The related runtime-stats precision issue is handled the same way in #113075, comparing peak stats in the tick domain instead of with a percentage window.

pthread barriers are used for something slightly different, where explicitly known threads need to align on a checkpoint before proceeding. They are kind of handy for some things.

Lazy init of mutex and condition variable resources is a bit of a side-effect to working around a number of things; differently sized mutexes across implementations, the fact that they can be (theoretically) either kernel or user objects (not strictly one or the other), and that mutexes are not futexes (which are limited to userspace and also nicely work on the stack too). Otherwise, we could use static initialization.

Because lazy init does not support static initialization (it's intentionally the opposite) it can create a bit of a race condition when an unknown number of threads try to use the same uninitialized object.

The structure here might be improved by only attempting to "get" an already initialized mutex outside of holding the semaphore.

The self-ownership check uses a hard-coded CPU-ID bitmask (`& 3U`), but spinlock validation encodes the CPU id in the low bits of `thread_cpu` with a mask that depends on pointer size (2 bits on 32-bit, 3 bits on 64-bit; see `kernel/spinlock_validate.c:10-12`). On 64-bit builds (arm64), `& 3U` will fail to match CPU IDs 4-7, so re-entrant printk on those CPUs can still recurse through spinlock validation instead of taking the intended fast-path.

Review: TLS Max Fragment Length socket option

* Two commits by Kacper Szkoda that make RFC 6066 Max Fragment Length (MFL) configurable per socket and let mbedTLS shrink its buffers post-handshake.

What they do

  0d001f82485 — modules: mbedtls: add MBEDTLS_SSL_VARIABLE_BUFFER_LENGTH Kconfig
  Exposes mbedTLS's MBEDTLS_SSL_VARIABLE_BUFFER_LENGTH. When on, in/out buffers are resized after the handshake down to the negotiated MFL + overhead, reducing per-connection footprint. Kconfig depends on !MBEDTLS_SSL_PROTO_TLS1_3 (MFL is TLS 1.2 only), plumbed into config-mbedtls.h.

  116a108c70b — net: sockets: tls: add TLS_MAX_FRAGMENT_LENGTH socket option
  New write-only sockopt ZSOCK_TLS_MAX_FRAGMENT_LENGTH with values ZSOCK_TLS_MFL_DISABLED/512/1024/2048/4096. Stored in a new int8_t options.mfl_code (default -1 = "use global"). tls_set_max_frag_len() now takes the whole tls_context and branches: per-socket override → direct map to mbedTLS code; 0 → suppress extension; -1 → old global behavior. Also removes the MBEDTLS_TLS_EXT_ADV_CONTENT_LEN < 16384 compile guard. Good test coverage (validation + real handshake negotiating 512/1024).

Correctness — the code is sound

* The direct mapping mfl_code (1-4) → mbedtls_ssl_conf_max_frag_len() is correct: ZSOCK_TLS_MFL_512..4096 happen to equal MBEDTLS_SSL_MAX_FRAG_LEN_512..4096 (1..4). This works but is an undocumented ABI coupling — worth a BUILD_ASSERT(ZSOCK_TLS_MFL_512 == MBEDTLS_SSL_MAX_FRAG_LEN_512 ...) so a future mbedTLS renumber can't silently break it.
* Input validation in tls_opt_mfl_set() is correct (null, optlen == sizeof(int), range [0,4]).
* No new races: mfl_code is set pre-handshake and consumed in tls_mbedtls_init(), same lifecycle as every other option.
* No memory-safety / info-disclosure / DoS concerns. Write-only option correctly falls through to -ENOPROTOOPT on getsockopt.

Findings worth raising

  1. Default-path behavior change at the 16384 boundary (functional regression risk). Removing the MBEDTLS_TLS_EXT_ADV_CONTENT_LEN < 16384 guard doesn't only affect the new override path — it also changes the mfl_code == -1 (default) path. Previously, a build with content length at the TLS max (16384) advertised no MFL extension, so peers could use full 16384-byte records. Now tls_mfl_code_from_content_len(16384) returns MAX_FRAG_LEN_4096, so those builds will advertise MFL_4096 and cap records at 4096 by default. The commit message justifies the removal for the override case ("true constraints enforced below"), but the side effect hits users who never set the sockopt. Consider keeping the < 16384 guard on the default branch and only bypassing it when mfl_code >= 0.

I think this trades a real bug for a systematic cost, and the bug is somewhere else.

A `CMCOR` of zero is a legitimate value. The compare matches on the next cycle, the ISR runs immediately, and that would correct itself on the spot, because the ISR announces and the kernel then asks for the next deadline. What makes it fatal here is the early return a few lines up:

```c
	/* Nothing to do when the kernel has no near deadline to schedule. */
	if (ticks == SYS_CLOCK_MAX_WAIT) {
		return;
	}
```

With an empty timeout queue the kernel passes exactly that value, so the driver declines to reprogram and whatever period is in place becomes permanent. That is what turns a zero into an interrupt storm rather than a single early tick. Your commit message says as much: "It does not self-heal either, because with no pending kernel timeout `sys_clock_set_timeout()` returns early on `SYS_CLOCK_MAX_WAIT` and never reprograms the register."

The clamp is not cheap on this SoC. `CYCLES_PER_TICK` is 60000, so `MIN_PERIOD_CYCLES` is 15000 cycles, 2.5 ms against a 10 ms tick. Because `MAX_TICKS` is 0 there, every `sys_clock_set_timeout()` asks for the distance to the next tick boundary, spread over one whole tick, so as much as a quarter of that range lands under the clamp and is pushed out. That is a permanent accuracy loss on the ordinary path, paid to contain one pathological value on the empty-queue path.

It is also worth noting that the early return is not conditioned on sloppy idle at all. Without that option `SYS_CLOCK_MAX_WAIT` is a genuine request: the kernel caps the wait there precisely so an announce lands within the range its tick accounting can represent. Declining to program it means the driver no longer honours that bound, and this patch does not address that either.

On this driver that is more than a range question, because the cycle base is extended by polling rather than by an interrupt. `cmt1_elapsed()` adds one CMT1 period when it notices the wrap flag, and catches a single wrap per call. CMT1 wraps every 65536 cycles, about 10.9 ms here, against a 10 ms tick, so the cycle count stays correct only while something calls that function often enough. Today that holds only because the period left behind in `CMCOR` happens to be short. It is not something the driver arranges, and it stops being true the moment a longer period is left in place, which is exactly the state the early return preserves.

Minor, but the description no longer matches the patch: it says "Push such a deadline out by a single cycle instead. The worst-case error is one cycle of jitter", which describes a different change from the quarter-tick clamp in the diff.

What I would suggest instead is fixing the reprogramming. In #114901 that early return is gone, and the no-deadline case has its own entry point which programs the longest period the register can hold:

[9e95394cb471](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/commit/9e95394cb471) in #114901

A `CMCOR` of zero then resolves at the next match: the ISR runs, the kernel reports nothing pending, and the driver stretches the period to `COUNTER_MAX`, 65535 cycles, which stays just inside the CMT1 wrap so the polling still catches every one. Short deadlines keep their accuracy, and the wakeup rate drops while nothing is pending, which the early return does not achieve either.

# Review: PR #115307 — net: if: don't leave mcast groups on iface down

- PR: https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/115307 (draft)
- Author: Fin Maaß <f.maass@vogl-electronic.com>
- Reviewed against: `main` at `f2b5ecd866f`
- Commits on the branch:
  1. `1ba58171e57` net: if: don't leave mcast groups on iface down (1 file, -43)
  2. `6de54ba21cc` net: dns: remove rejoin (4 files, +8 -216)

## Verdict

The bug that commit 1 targets is real and worth fixing. The commit is not
ready as it stands: it breaks an existing mDNS runtime-control test and it
leaves offloaded and point-to-point interfaces without any join or leave
notification across a down/up cycle.

Commit 2 does not compile in `CONFIG_MDNS_RESPONDER_PROBE=y` builds and
removes recovery behaviour that is still needed. It should be dropped or
reduced to a much smaller change.

## The underlying bug is real

`net_if_down()` calls `net_ipv6_mld_leave()` / `net_ipv4_igmp_leave()`. Those
do not merely mark the group unjoined, they call `net_if_ipv6_maddr_rm()` /
`net_if_ipv4_maddr_rm()`, which drop a reference and free the record when the
count reaches zero:

```c
int net_ipv6_mld_leave(struct net_if *iface, const struct net_in6_addr *addr)
{
	...
	removed_addr = maddr->address;
	if (!net_if_ipv6_maddr_rm(iface, addr)) {
		/* Address still in use */
		return 0;
	}
```

Recovery on the way back up is `rejoin_multicast_groups()`, which only walks
entries whose `is_used` flag is still set, so a freed record can never come
back. An application's `IPV6_ADD_MEMBERSHIP` / `IP_ADD_MEMBERSHIP` is
therefore destroyed by an administrative down, with no way for the
application to notice or recover through the socket API. The report is
accurate.

There is a second, quieter consequence that the commit message does not
mention. When two sockets joined the same group the record is not freed, but
the reference count is still decremented, so the accounting is left
permanently wrong and a later leave by one socket removes the group while the
other still expects membership.

Note that the operational-down path is already correct: `notify_iface_down()`
calls `clear_joined_ipv{4,6}_mcast_groups()`, which only clears `is_joined`
and keeps the record, and `notify_iface_up()` calls
`rejoin_multicast_groups()`. Commit 1 makes the administrative path behave the
same way. That symmetry is a good argument for the change and belongs in the
commit message.

## Findings — commit 1

### 1. Breaks `test_runtime_disable_then_enable_iface` (blocking)

`net.mdns.runtime_iface_allowlist::test_runtime_disable_then_enable_iface`
fails with commit 1 applied on its own:

```
Expectation failed at tests/net/lib/mdns_responder/src/main.c:1154:
	(ipv4_group_joined(iface1) is true)
	iface1 still in the IPv4 mDNS group after disable
Expectation failed at tests/net/lib/mdns_responder/src/main.c:1156:
	(ipv6_group_joined(iface1) is true)
	iface1 still in the IPv6 mDNS group after disable
```

Instrumenting the group reference count at that point:

| | ref before disable | ref after disable |
| --- | --- | --- |
| baseline | 1 | -1 (record freed) |
| commit 1 | 2 | 1 (still joined) |

The responder joins the group again when its listener is re-initialised after
the interface comes up. That join used to recreate a freed record at one
reference; with the patch it adds a second reference to a record that
survived. The single leave in `mdns_responder_disable_iface()` then no longer
removes the interface from the group, so the responder keeps receiving mDNS
traffic on an interface the application explicitly disabled.

The existing `test_ipv{4,6}_group_ref_not_leaked_on_cycles` tests still pass,
so this is not an unbounded leak per cycle, but the balance is wrong. Either
the responder must not join again while it already holds a reference, or the
disable path must drop every reference it holds.

### 2. No MLD Done / IGMP Leave is sent anymore (needs a decision)

Commit 1 removes the only place that emits a Done / Leave on administrative
down, so nothing tells the querier or an IGMP/MLD-snooping switch that the
node stopped listening; the switch has to age the state out. Linux keeps the
membership across a link down but still sends the leave. Dropping the message
may well be acceptable here, since the interface is being disabled anyway and
it makes the administrative path match the carrier path, but the commit
message should say so explicitly instead of being silent about it.

### 3. Incomplete for offloaded and point-to-point interfaces (should fix)

`notify_iface_down()` and `notify_iface_up()` both skip `clear_joined_*` and
`rejoin_multicast_groups()` for offloaded and `NET_L2_POINT_TO_POINT`
interfaces:

```c
	if (!net_if_is_offloaded(iface) &&
	    !(l2_flags_get(iface) & NET_L2_POINT_TO_POINT)) {
		rejoin_multicast_groups(iface);
		...
```

For those interfaces the old destructive leave at least called
`net_if_mcast_monitor(..., false)`, which is how offloaded drivers program
their hardware multicast filters. After the patch such an interface cycles
down and up with no monitor callback at all, so a Wi-Fi driver that clears its
filter on down never gets it restored, and `is_joined` stays set so the core
rejoin skips it as well. This is the platform where mDNS matters most.

### 4. No test (should fix)

Nothing in the tree covers the case the PR is actually about: a plain socket
keeping its `IP_ADD_MEMBERSHIP` / `IPV6_ADD_MEMBERSHIP` across an
administrative down and up. The mDNS suite only passes today because the
responder carries its own rejoin workaround, which commit 2 then removes.

## Findings — commit 2

### 5. Does not build with `CONFIG_MDNS_RESPONDER_PROBE=y` (blocking)

```c
net_mgmt_init_event_callback(&mgmt_iface_cb, NET_EVENT_IF_UP, flags);
```

The handler and event-mask arguments are swapped, and the `uint64_t flags`
local was deleted in the same hunk. `tests/net/lib/mdns_responder_probe`
errors out with `error: flags undeclared (first use in this function)`.

### 6. Removes recovery that is still needed (blocking)

`test_ipv4_igmp_report_when_already_joined_on_if_up` fails in all five mDNS
configurations. That test covers the case where the group is still marked
joined when `NET_EVENT_IF_UP` arrives and a fresh membership report must be
emitted anyway, so that a snooping switch which dropped its state during the
outage starts forwarding again. Commit 1 does not address this: a plain join
returns early when the group is already joined, and the core rejoin only fires
for entries that `clear_joined_*` unmarked.

On offloaded and point-to-point interfaces the responders' `IF_UP` handler is
the only recovery path at all, since the core skips those (finding 3).

The premise of commit 2 — that the rejoin is no longer needed — therefore
holds only for native interfaces that went through a full operational down.
In every other case it deletes the recovery. The same argument applies to the
`llmnr_responder.c` handler and to `mdns_rejoin_groups()` in `resolve.c`,
which covers the `MDNS_RESOLVER && !MDNS_RESPONDER` configuration.

| `tests/net/igmp` | pass | pass | pass |
| `tests/net/lib/mdns_responder` | pass (5 configs) | 1 failure | 6 failures in 5 configs |
| `tests/net/lib/llmnr_responder` | pass | pass | pass |

```
net.mdns.runtime_iface_allowlist.test_mdns_responder.runtime_disable_then_enable_iface
```

## Commit message notes

Both subjects should follow the Zephyr convention of a capitalised imperative
after the area prefix, for example `net: if: Do not leave mcast groups on
iface down`. The body of commit 1 is written in the first person as an issue
report ("When I set the socket option ... I expect"); it should describe the
change, why it is correct, and how it was tested. `net: dns: remove rejoin` is
too terse to review from the message alone.

## Recommendation

Drop commit 2, or reduce it to removing only the `-ENOENT` fallback that
existed purely because the record used to be destroyed, keeping the rejoin

Keep commit 1, but fix the mDNS double-join so runtime disable keeps working,
decide and document what happens to offloaded and point-to-point interfaces,
and add a socket-level test for a membership surviving an administrative
down/up.

>
> **Examples**
>
> * **Buffer underflow**: a decoder requested 1024 bytes, but only 200 were available.

With `A = Z_LOG_MSG_ALIGNMENT`, the current expression is equivalent to:

```
p = alloca(_size + A - 1);

```

So the extra `A - 1` is already part of the size passed to `alloca()`, as required. Since rounding advances `p` by at most `A - 1`, at least

```
_size + A - 1 - (A - 1) = _size
```

bytes remain available from `q`. And by definition of `ROUND_UP()`, `q` is aligned to `A`.

As far as I can see, one case I don't see covered in the PR or the discussion so far: modems where GNSS and LTE share the RF path and are mutually exclusive. On the HL78xx, GNSS can only be used when the module is not actively connected on LTE/GSM. - GNSS is running and the app calls net_if_up(): does the modem driver run the GNSS shutdown first, or refuse?

When FTQ remains set after the 1 ms bound, the queue has not been confirmed flushed, but the code still reinitializes the descriptor ring, restarts DMA, and then releases the packet/buffer references. If the DMA is still active, it can follow the new ring or write into buffers that have already returned to the pool. Keep TX stopped and perform a full reset or record a failed state until DMA quiescence is guaranteed before releasing these resources.

The backport hands the descriptors to DMA by setting OWN without a memory barrier. `volatile` only constrains compiler ordering; on the Cortex-M AXI path the DMA can observe OWN before the buffer/control words are visible, causing intermittent corrupt TX. Add a DMB before the OWN writes and a DSB after them before publishing the tail pointer.
